utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with my learned friend Mrs Teresa McHenry and Miss Elles van Dusschoten and support assistant Mr Rod Dixon. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The appearances for the defence, please. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel of Zejnil Delalic being together with Mr Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor of criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am Michael Greaves, counsel on behalf of Mr Mucic. MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): I am Salih Karabdic, counsel of the accused Mr Hazim Delic, and with me in the team is Mr Thomas Moran, lawyer from Houston, Texas. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Mustafa Brackovic, defence counsel of the fourth accused, Esad Landzo, and with me in the defence team is Mrs Cynthia McMurrey, who probably was not informed of the earlier start of this morning's sessions. utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY

utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I believe they were shown and identified to the witness yesterday and I do not believe there will be any dispute with counsel that the witness statements they were referring to, although they did not themselves mark them, are the witness statements of Mrs Cecez, but ... JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not quite understand this. Which of the defence counsel was trying to put it in then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were not trying to put it in, but we referred to it several times and showed it to the witness, and certainly we should have objected more vigorously at the time and made sure they were marked and introduced into evidence, but given that I do not believe that there is any dispute that these are her prior statements that the defence counsel referred to, and indeed showed the witness, we believe that they may be introduced into evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Did it not occur to you during re-examination to put it to her?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for my defects in not raising this issue earlier, and I realise it is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, I had pointed out yesterday that these documents should be brought into the evidence and it was not done at that stage. I thought you were quite happy they should not be brought into the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I thought after you brought it up the defence would do it, and then, because I must admit I was confused by the whole manner in which the defence was doing it, I neglected to do it, which is why on the theory better late than never I am attempting to offer them into evidence now. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is a little awkward. Can I hear the defence on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Tom Moran for Hasim Delic. A couple of thoughts, your Honour. First, there are some questions based on the witness's testimony as to the authenticity of one of the documents. There was a document -- there was a record of a court proceeding in the former Yugoslavia, and there was some corrections made to that record in handwriting, and the witness said she did not recall anything at all about those corrections, but, more importantly, your Honour, if the court wishes to have those introduced into evidence, we wish they be admitted solely for the limited purpose of impeachment rather than for all purposes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, that is the only basis on which it could be admitted in the first instance, but if it was not so done then ... since Mr Moran is not objecting to that you can tender is at least for impeachment purposes if it has any such effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Except the document with the corrections on it because there is some question based on the witness's testimony as to the authenticity of the corrections. It is the court record from a proceeding before an administrative -- an investigating magistrate in the former Yugoslavia. There are two versions of it. One of them is the original version and the other is the version with corrections, and, as the court will recall, I asked the witness will the corrections and she said she did not recall anything about them. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What I remember is, as she said, she came to The Hague only once, only once, and that she did not remember any of the corrections made in the second version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is what she said. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr President, I do not know in what way the witness could now authenticate one of the documents of which she said that she had not even given it. Therefore, there are several statements we are talking about, incorrect statements, statements given elsewhere in a different place and statements that the witness claims never to have made. Therefore, the only basis for accepting this in evidence could be to impeach the witness and to impeach the procedure by which the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are talking about the document which admittedly bore her signatures and admittedly contained corrections in her own handwriting. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually there is no doubt about what is being discussed. Mr Moran, who started it, put that document to her. She denied knowing about how the mistakes were corrected. This is what the prosecution now wants tendered, at least for impeachment purposes and for no other thing. I think that is sufficient for that purpose. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, as defence counsel of Esad Landzo, I should like to support what has been said by counsel Edina Residovic. I also support all the reasons she has given, so I do not feel it necessary to elaborate on them. The authenticity of the statement may be called in question, and especially of the corrections made subsequently, and the witness in her statement gave a wrong location, and she also could not remember having made that statement, and therefore we are absolutely against the acceptance of this statement as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as Mr Mucic is concerned, the position is this, that I am content to adopt the arguments advanced by each of my friends who appear for the defence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think after listening to all that has been said I am content to admitting for the purposes of impeaching whatever has been said on the opposing statements, because there are two statements which Mr Moran did consider, and I think that is the only purpose for which that document is being tendered. I think it is admissible for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. I believe there were a total of three separate statements, plus the one with corrections. Are all four being admitted for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The one relating to the -- we are talking about the document which she admitted bore her signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is the one. We would ask if one be admitted, they all be admitted for the purposes of impeachment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That was not what was in issue yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is an objection to it because you have to confront the witness with the omissions or contradictions. You referred the witness only to that particular document which bore her signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So that is the only one that is in issue, not all the others. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr President, I asked the witness to recognise the statement, which she did not recognise as having made. Therefore, we would ask that all the statements be tendered together. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You are raising quite fresh issues different from what the prosecution has related to us, and I think I am only considering the issue the prosecution raised as compared with the evidence which Mr Moran was concerned with. All that is new and I do not think anybody is thinking about that now. We do not use this opportunity to raise new things other than what the prosecution has said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may apologise to the court for being tardy this morning. I would also like to add that, because we had discussed our strategy and because we had assumed that this document would not have been introduced into evidence, Esad Landzo waived questioning of that witness completely. Now, if this document is admitted into evidence, then we would like to ask the court's indulgence to reopen cross-examination just for the limited purpose of that document only, nothing further. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not remember the document being in issue at any time. All it was used at that time was for the purposes of cross-examining the witness. That was what was done. So its admission was never an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The defence itself introduced that document by referring to it in the cross-examination of the witness. It was not the prosecution which has done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I understand that is correct but our defence agreement was basically the document would not be admitted into evidence, but I can see our hands are tied at this point. I wanted to express to the court that if it is allowed into evidence, defence or prosecution, Esad Landzo has a few questions to clear up on that one statement, and we would like to have just a tiny bit of cross limited to five questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It might be impossible to allow you that indulgence, because it is merely being tendered for the purposes of impeaching that document. So it has nothing to do with your opportunity of cross-examining. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will now tender them into evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Only one. I do not remember more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I believe it is the document that was -- she said had taken place in Borci. I will tender both the document and the translation of it. It is the document that was given to defence counsel yesterday morning. If I understand correctly. Thank you. I have anything else if anyone wants it. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Will you kindly invite the witness? (Witness enters court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly take your seat. Please remind her she is still on her oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I wish to remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr Marie-Janine Calic (continued) Examined by Mr Ostberg

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr Calic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we went so far as to document number 7 in your file of documents. I hope today that all the counsel have their files with them. The court has them before them, I can see. So we do not have to take up time putting documents on the ELMO except for maybe maps or things like that. May I ask you, Dr Calic, to take up the thread where you left it yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me briefly summarise what I was trying to explain yesterday. Basically there were two subjects of debate among the leaderships of the people in Bosnia. One was the question of independence of Bosnia and the second was the future constitutional set-up of Bosnia. Both questions were, of course, interlinked and this is what made it difficult for the leaderships to agree on a common view. As far as the question of independence, there was an alliance between the Croat leadership and the Muslim leadership. Both did not want to stay in a Yugoslav state which would have probably been dominated by the Serbs. That is why they were in favour of independence, but as for the second question there was a different coalition. There was a coalition between the Croat and the Serb leadership. As for the question of the future constitution, both were in favour of having a constitution on the basis of ethnic principles, cantonisation. Instead the Muslim leadership was in favour of having a unitarian state. This is what I was trying to explain yesterday. The Bosnian Serbs continued to contest the legitimacy of the Sarajevo Assembly, having decided to become -- Bosnia to become an independent and sovereign state, and from September onwards they made a number of decisions. They were trying to establish their own state. I have included in this file a number of documents showing how the Serbs were then trying to establish their own state, the government, the constitution. These are the documents number 7 -- from number 7 to 15, and if you allow me, your Honours, I would prefer not to show each document but just two of them. These documents seem for me important for two reasons. One is document number 10. It indicates the territories which the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted to include in the Serb state of Bosnia. It's just a bit difficult here. We can see from this document, which numbers all the municipalities who were supposed to become part of the Bosnian Serb republic. Can we switch on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have some help from any technician with the ELMO? . Now we see the model on the screen and not the document. There we are. Are you directing our interest to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this Decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this document you find all the municipalities which were supposed to become part of the Serbian Republic, Serb Republic of Bosnia, and we can see from this document that Konjic was not supposed to be part of this republic. So the Serbs proclaimed in January the republic of the Serbian people. They declared a constitution in February and they declared independence from Bosnia in April 1992. Let me emphasise that in many of these documents the Serbs expressed their wish to stay in Yugoslavia, so they considered themselves as being part of what remained of Yugoslavia. The constitutional court of Bosnia instead made two decisions declaring these unconstitutional, and I have also included the decisions of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia in this file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's number 16 and 17. The Bosnian Serbs were not the only group challenging the territorial integrity of Bosnia. Also the Bosnian Croats were moving towards independence. In November 1991 the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Sava Valley was established and in November Croat leaders decided to form the so-called Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. This community of Herceg-Bosnia was defined as a political, cultural, economic and regional entity, and on 3rd July 1992 it was officially proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what we find under number 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what you find under number 18 and in this document, which I also will show you a bit in detail we can recognise under Article -- I cannot see it on my screen -- under Article 2 we can read: "The Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna shall consist of the following municipalities..." We can see here that Konjic was supposed to become part of this republic -- not republic. It was called "community", but in fact it was perceived as a separate state and this is also exactly how the constitutional court in Sarajevo perceived this declaration of the Croat -- proclamation of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. They also made a Decision against this declaring Herceg-Bosna unconstitutional. This is document number 19 in my folder. Let us go back to what happened in autumn 1991. In October I was explaining yesterday there was a proclamation, declaration of sovereignty by the Bosnian Assembly. There was Serb opposition against this declaration. There was a break-up of all state institutions in Bosnia and there was a letter by the Bosnian government to the European Community in December 1991. Bosnia should be recognised as an independent republic. In view of these facts tensions in Bosnia increased constantly throughout the winter of 1991/1992 reaching a peak after the referendum on 29th February and 1st March 1992 on the republic's independence. The European Community had made independence -- had made recognition of Bosnia conditional on holding a referendum to determine whether the population of Bosnia was really in favour of independence. This brings me back to the Badinter Commission, which I mentioned yesterday. This time it is Opinion Number 4, document number 20 in our file. Can we have it on the screen? So the European Community Arbitration Commission under Badinter was aware of the fact that a part of the Bosnian population was opposing independence. You can see this in the last page which is on the screen, paragraph 4: "It was therefore of the opinion that the will of the people of Bosnia to constitute an independent republic, an independent state, cannot be held to have been fully established." This is what they were assessing. In the referendum, it was the condition of the European Community to recognise independence. 66 per cent of the Bosnian citizens participated. The Serbs boycotted this referendum and the overwhelming majority of those who took part -- this is nearly 66 per cent of the Bosnian population -- expressed their will that Bosnia should become indeed an independent state. The European Community then took the decision to recognise Bosnia and from 7th April 1992 Bosnia was a sovereign independent republic recognised by the European Community, by the United States, and other states followed. Even before the official recognition of Bosnia around the referendum the first violent incidents occurred in Bosnia, and the European Community was very concerned about this fact. The first barricades were set up in Sarajevo. There were violent incidents, and you can see these events from a declaration, document number 22, a statement of the European Union. I will not put it on the screen. It is just to support what I am saying. So the referendum maybe was the turning point towards a more violent state in this republic. Bigger, more violent conflicts erupted after Bosnia became independent, and the Presidency of Bosnia had to declare the state of imminent war danger on 8th April 1992, which meant that all power was now concentrated in the Presidency. The Parliament did not work any more. First efforts to mobilise soldiers were undertaken. The state of war was proclaimed by the state Presidency as late as June 1992, nearly three months after the break-out of armed hostility. There was a certain period in which -- during which the Bosnian Presidency was acting under immediate danger of war but not under a state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any explanation to why it took more than two months to come up with the decision of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many speculations. I am personally not sure about the real reasons for this. It is, on the other hand, a fact that the difference between having immediate -- a state of immediate war danger and having a state of war danger are not too big in terms of mobilising all forces against the perceived enemy. So the real reason I cannot know this or I cannot support with any document this -- I mean it is just speculation, but it was a matter of criticism. It has been criticised from various sides that it took so long to organise all forces against this perceived enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during this period in shaping a Bosnian army? You are coming to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am coming now and I am moving to the main military forces in the Republic of Bosnia. I am also explaining how the Bosnian army was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main military forces which were active in Bosnia in 1992 need to be described in the context of the Yugoslav defence doctrine of all people's defence, also known as total national defence. It is just a question how to translate this Yugoslav term. So all people's defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what is called TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The doctrine is all -- I will explain what is TO, but all people's defence meant the Yugoslav defence doctrine, which was introduced in 1968, and it was meant and aimed to mobilise all possible means and resources from the bottom up of the society upwards to the purpose of defence in the event of war. It meant also that practically all citizens were expected to participate in armed struggle wherever they could. This doctrine was implemented in the defence law of 1969 and later on in the defence law of 1974, and we can also find it in the constitutions of Bosnia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In its Article 254 the constitution of Bosnia referred explicitly to the principle of all people's defence. I quote: "It is the right of the working people and citizens to actively participate in the formulation of defence policy and preparations for the defence of the country, and to ensure themselves within the framework of the system and plans for national defence, the conditions necessary for training to protect and defend the country, and to participate in its defence." The Yugoslav system of all people's defence had basically three main components. One component was civil protection, the Civil Protection Organisation, as it was called. This was an organisation aimed to provide relief in the case of war for civilians, but also in the case of natural disasters. I am not going too far and not explaining too much on this. More interesting for us are the other two elements, the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav people's army was one part of the armed forces and the so-called territorial defence organisation, TO, was the second element of this defence of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav people's army known under the name of JNA was the regular standing army of Yugoslavia. It was the federal army. It was also financed by the federal budget and it existed since 1945. The Territorial Defence Organisation, on the other hand, was under the authority, control and jurisdiction of the republic as a second pillar of the Yugoslav defence system. So since 1968 the armed forces of Yugoslavia were composed of JNA as a federal army and of the territorial defence organisations as the armies of the republics. Each republic had its own headquarters of the territorial defence, TO, which was responsible to the respective republican presidency in a military sense, but in a political sense there was also a certain responsibility towards Belgrade, towards the federal army, because this system of defence was conceived as a unified system, and this is how it should have worked in the case of war. I would like to show you my document 28 just to make visible how the armed forces of Yugoslavia were structured. This comes from Zivkovic on the Territorial Defence of Yugoslavia printed in Belgrade in 1985. You can here see forces of Yugoslavia. First pillar: the Yugoslav people's army, JNA; second pillar: Territorial Defence Organisation under the jurisdiction of the republic. The Federal Army of Yugoslavia, JNA was the largest and best equipped armed force in the armed conflicts that began in Yugoslavia in 1991. The JNA was a real pan-Yugoslavian institution deriving from Second World War partition and struggle against German and Italian occupation. So it was the one army which was aiming at, let us say, at least in this early part of the war -- aiming at keeping Yugoslavia together as a state. However, as the first armed conflicts erupted, the JNA turned more and more -- it became more and more a Serb-dominated force. Many of non-Serb officers left the army. They were joining the local territorial defence units and you have to see that the JNA as early as the autumn of 1991 started mobilising also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially Bosnian Serbs, and they started also distributing weapons to Bosnian Serb volunteers. So as early as the autumn of 1991 we can conclude that the JNA was becoming more and more a Serb-dominated army. All parties to the conflict were arming their respective populations, and this was again a matter of concern. On the international level the United Nations Security Council passed a resolution in September 1991 imposing an arms embargo on the whole territory of Yugoslavia. I included the Security Council resolution, but it is a well-known fact. I think there is no need that I put it here on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can find it in your binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can find it in the binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA was openly present and it was also involved in the armed struggles in Bosnia-Herzegovina at least until May 1992. On 4th May the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which consisted at that time of Serbia and Montenegro decided to withdraw JNA troops from Bosnia, withdraw the troops from Bosnia by 19th May 1992. During this formal withdrawal, however, the JNA left behind many of their troops and also equipment and arms. These former JNA forces, armed with heavy weaponry, were integrated in the newly-established Bosnian Serb Army, which was later to become the army of the Republika Srpska. This is a process which General Veljko Kadijevic of JNA described in his book "Moje Vidjenje Raspada", "My View on the Collapse", as follows. You have this document 31 in the binder. Let me put it on the ELMO. It is such an interesting quote can we see it on the screen, please? It is this paragraph basically, in which he openly admits that: "The units and headquarters of the JNA formed the backbone of the army of the Serb Republic with complete weaponry and equipment".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I put a question to you in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you just said about JNA, what they left in the territory of Bosnia, would that mean that after the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina hostile forces belonging to another republic was fighting on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is indeed true, and there is much evidence that the JNA remained involved in the struggles in Bosnia even after May 1992. We have quite a lot of evidence for this. I included one document, which is a report of the UN Secretary General of 3rd December 1992, document 32, again expressing concern about the fact that, despite the decision to withdraw the JNA, JNA troops were still present and at least actively supporting the Bosnian Serb army in this armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the territory of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the territory of Bosnia. The idea to recognise Bosnia as an independent state and to recognise also Croatia was originally to transform the conflict into an international conflict. This was aimed to deter the Yugoslav army to be involved in the two republics, but it did not work, as we can see from these documents and from any other documents. See also report of UN Secretary General of 3rd December 1992, document 32 in this binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So how many were the Bosnian Serb troops? Difficult to say. There are very different assessments. Most scholars estimated at that time there were about 60,000, but it could easily be more or less. During the conflict they were mobilising more troops, reaching then during 1993 maybe up to 100,000 troops, reserve troops included, but there is no reliable -- not really one document showing how many they really were. So far to the Bosnian Serb army. What we are doing now, the Bosnian Muslims, respectively the Bosnian government. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we might rise now, have a break and reassemble at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. (11.07 am) (Short break) (11.30 am) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please remind the witness she is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Well, Dr Calic, I just ask you to continue before you stopped before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started to describe how the unified system of all people's defence started to disintegrate when the first armed conflict erupted in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992. I also identified two main military actors on the republican level. One was the JNA on its way out of Bosnia and the second one was the Bosnian Serb Army, which was formed in May 1992, and, as I was explaining, they included part of the JNA troops, personnel, arms, equipment and so on. So the third important actor in this war is the Bosnian Army itself. The Bosnian Army was created in April 1992. The basic organisation was the Territorial Defence Organisation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the so-called second pillar of the former unified former system of Yugoslavia. The Bosnian presidency announced mobilisation of the Territorial Defence Organisation in April 1992. Territorial defence units were mobilised in many municipalities throughout BH including Konjic municipality. The Presidency of Bosnia set up a Supreme Command in Sarajevo, and they were also trying to set up regional headquarters. These headquarters were situated, among others, in Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Doboj and in Bihac. The formal date of establishment of the Bosnian Army is 15th April 1992. There was also a decree on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia passed in May. It is also included in this binder. The Bosnian Army was conceived as the common armed forces of all three constitutive peoples of the Republic of Bosnia and it was under the command and control of the Bosnian Presidency. However, as I was trying to describe earlier on, many members of other -- of non-Muslim nationalities did not follow this order. They did not become part of this Bosnian Army, but they were trying to establish their own order forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put the question to you in this context. What you have just said about the forming of the Bosnian Army, would that mean that when the attacks against the villages surrounding Konjic took place in May 1992 there was also a Bosnian Army formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On paper, yes. There was a Bosnian Army formed, but I will explain later on that many of the regulations which were passed in April and in May 1992 by the Bosnian Presidency and by the Bosnian government were not implemented in practice. So there were many parts of Bosnia -- in many parts of Bosnia the local units were acting practically independently from their supposed superior command, but I will explain this later on in more detail, when I come to what happened in Konjic during this early period of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So how many were now the troops of the Bosnian Army? Again we have the problem in this early period. There were different sources. Different sources say different things. Between 50,000 and 80,000 and then during the war up to 100,000 personnel. Anyway, we have to acknowledge that even maybe if the Bosnian Army were more in personnel in numbers, they were for sure not sufficiently armed and they were unequipped. This was maybe one of the main problems of the newly-established Bosnian Army. Another problem was, as I was already pointing out before, that not all troops were actually following the orders given by the Bosnian Presidency to build up the new Bosnian Army, but they were creating their own armed forces. The Bosnian Serb Army was one, but also the Croats established their own armed forces. This brings me to the next important actor, the Croatian Defence Council, HVO. The Croatian armed forces were established in April 1992 together with separate headquarters, and they were conceived to be the armed forces of the Bosnian Croats. From the very beginning the armed forces of the Bosnian Croats, the HVO, had quite good relations with the Bosnian army. The HVO comprised of some 30,000 troops, most of them trained and armed by the government of Croatia, and this brings me to a second external actor in the Bosnian war. We have also many reports from the international organisations, showing how the Croatian army from Croatia was involved actively and took part in the Bosnian war. This is, for instance, my document number 37, the report of the UN Secretary-General of 24th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention from which time the Croat influence was to be observed on the Bosnian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was practically to be observed from when the HVO was established. We can say there were some signs already in late 1991 but there were many more signs in 1992, when the conflict actually erupted, the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So let us summarise the main actors on the republican level, the JNA, the Bosnian Serb Army, the HVO, the Croatian armed forces, and of course the Bosnian Army established in April 1992. Let me now come to the micro level and look in more detail at what happened then in the municipalities, as Konjic was one of the Yugoslav -- the Bosnian municipalities. I prepared a map showing 109 municipalities of Bosnia. Can we have it on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have this in the bundle also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have it in the binder, number 38. Can it be reduced? ? So 109 municipalities. Konjic is located here. We can see the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo. Here is the coast. Here lies Croatia and here the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia in socialist times granted the municipalities quite a high level of autonomy, and this was to prevent the emergence of political and ethnic tensions. The aim was to provide self-government, of course always in the framework of the federal and of the republican supervision. Article 116 of the Yugoslav constitution of 1974 stated: "A commune" of the municipality "is a self-managing community and the basic socio-political community based on the power of and self-management by the working class and all working people." According to the Yugoslav constitution, the municipalities had, among others, the rights and the duties to take care of economic, cultural, social and other common needs of the Yugoslav citizens. They were also allowed to set up organs of self-management and organs of power for the conduct of such affairs, and they were also enabled to regulate and to organise national defence and, of course, self-protection, and this brings me to the very essence of our case here. Before I come to what happened in Konjic, let me just show another diagram. This is the diagram number 40. I will not explain it in too much detail. It is the former Yugoslavian organisation of the municipalities. Just briefly to mention which bodies on the political side were set up in the Bosnian municipalities to organise self-administration, and who "the authorities" were at that time. So we can find an Assembly, Municipal Assembly, which was elected. In the municipality there was an Executive Council, which functioned more or less as a kind of local government, so it was the council, but there was also a President of the Municipal Assembly, and this President performed maybe the highest function in a municipality. He was in charge of organisational questions related to the work of the Assembly and related to the work of the council, and he held at the same time the position of co-ordinator and supervisor of the different institutions of the municipality. So this was basically how municipality was functioning before the war. Assembly with different chambers, self-management, quasi-government and not seen here on this graph but this high position of President of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This organogram, Dr Calic, is taken from a book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is taken from a book by Aleksandar Ivic and a co-author. It is named "Political and Constitutional System of the SFRY" published in Belgrade in 1988. It is a book on administration and constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What interests us here is that the municipalities played an important role in implementing the doctrine of all people's defence, all people's defence, which meant to mobilise all possible persons, means and resources from the local level upwards in case of a war. The municipality was conceived as an autonomous community of defence; in other words, a kind of nucleus of national resistance against foreign invasion. This is how it was meant, but then during the war in Bosnia it changed this meaning, and it became a completely different thing. In terms of the 1974 Bosnian constitution, the municipalities were able to make certain decisions in the event of a war or an imminence of war. Article 273 of the Bosnian constitution stated and I quote: "In time of war or in case of an immediate threat of war the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly shall be formed, will decide questions within the competence of the Assembly if it is impossible for the Assembly to meet.2. We have the exact articles of the Bosnian constitution in document 25, which explains the functions of the War Presidency in times of war. It was Article 273. I will come back later to this in more detail, when I explain exactly what happened in Konjic, but at this stage it is enough to bear in mind that municipalities played indeed a very important role in self-defence, and that they were allowed under the constitution of Yugoslavia and under the constitution of Bosnia to perform certain war-related tasks. So how was this now implemented in Konjic? Let me show first some basic data on the municipality of Konjic. First, a diagram of the ethnic composition of Konjic municipalities in 1991, document number 42. I will put it on the screen on the ELMO. I cannot see it on the screen. Maybe you can. Do we have it on the screen? Okay. Can you reduce it a bit? Thank you. In 1991 the population of Konjic municipality was composed of 54 per cent Muslims, 26 per cent Croats, 15 per cent were Serbs and 3 per cent were Yugoslavs, and then there were also 1 per cent of population of other nationalities. The population was 43,000 altogether approximately. So this is how it was in 1991. I will at the end of my statement show another diagram. This diagram will then show the ethnic composition of today. So we have about 15 per cent Serbs in this municipalities, 6,620 people. Let us look how these people were distributed. Another map, document 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the population census of 1991. We can see that also the municipality of Konjic was mixed and you can see majority villages of the Muslims nearly all over this municipalities. The red ones are the Serbs. So there is no clear division within this municipality. There are no clear Muslim or no clear only Serb areas in this municipality. Let us look, however, where the Serbs, Serb villages, the Serb majority villages were located. Let me put document number 43, a map of the Serb towns of the municipality of Konjic. So these are the settlements with Serbs as an absolute majority. We can see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly how do I read this? The blue dots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The blue points, dots, they are the settlements with Serbs as absolute majority. Interestingly these villages were located along the main road running from Sarajevo down to the coast and along the railway, running also along mainly the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In document 44, which I will also put on the screen, we can see a bit better where Konjic was located, mainly in the northern part of Herzegovina. Here in the northern part is Sarajevo. Here is the coast. Much of its area is heavily wooded. It is rocky, it is mountainous and this makes it difficult to carry out any land operation. Konjic is located on the Neretva river in the valley of the Neretva but it has high mountains around. The whole area is important as a transit region for several reasons. There are important communication lines. I also mentioned the road and the railway from Sarajevo down to the coast, but there were also other important communication lines very close to the municipality of Konjic: the road here from Jablanica going up to Gorni Vakuf, Central Bosnia, and other roads leading from this main road through Herzegovina to the eastern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Central Bosnia, which starts -- Konjic is also something like the border between the two historical areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's the most important municipality of Herzegovina and it is so very close to an area which we call Central Bosnia, and which then starts from here up. During the Second World War Bosnia, especially Central and eastern Bosnia, witnessed very bitter ethnic struggles. During the Second World War Bosnia formed part of the Croat fascist state. Under the so-called Ustasha the fascist state was established by the German regime. It had the name of an independent state but it was not an independent state. It was occupied territory. So Bosnia was part of this state and so was Konjic. The Croat fascists during this time conducted an extremely brutal war against the Serbs. Hundreds of thousands of Serbs were killed in this time and, of course, this history is still in the minds of the people in this area. There were also Serb nationalists conducting aggressions against non-Serbs, and this Cetnik, the national movement of Cetniks, of course, massacred thousands of Muslims and Croats in this area. There is a whole debate over how many people were really killed during this struggle. It is a matter of debate among historians in the countries of the former Yugoslavia. It is a highly politicised debate. All sides claim to have more victims on their side. Being a historian looking from the outside, having seen many sources, I would conclude that there were altogether 1 million Yugoslavs who died, Yugoslavs all over Yugoslavia who died during the Second World War and Bosnia lost about 10 per cent of its population. So this is just to give a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Bosnian population", do you mean all three nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 10 per cent of the total population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Population, yes. Historically Konjic and also the Neretva River marks the border-line between two historic spheres of influence. For historical reasons the Bosnian Croats and also the Croatian Croats have laid claim to Herzegovina, which they consider as the real heartland of Croatian. Herzegovina goes up to here, the Mt Ivan saddle, which marks the border between Herzegovina and Bosnia. They have laid claim to this territory for historical reasons, even though there are many, many municipalities and areas where Croats are not in the majority but where the Muslims are in a majority. The Serb leadership, on the other hand, apparently had territorial aspirations on the eastern side of the Neretva Valley. It was reported in the press that since the beginning of the war, the Serb leadership considered territory east of this Neretva Valley as being Serb territory. There is no document evidence. This is just press reports. There were also many, many speculations that the Serb and the Croat Presidents and the local leaders of the Croats and the Serbs had made an agreement to divide Bosnia between themselves, and we find the municipality of Konjic in the middle of this. So on the one side the Serb aspiration and the Croats, and nothing left for the Bosnian Muslims. So for all these reasons, as well as for others, which I will discuss now, the Konjic municipality has been of high strategic importance for all the warring factions. I mentioned the strategically very important road running from Sarajevo down to the coast. It was a major line of supply for the Bosnian troops. I have also to mention that Sarajevo was besieged from the very beginning of the conflict, and this was the way through which -- this was the way from Central Bosnia and from Herzegovina to reach Sarajevo from the western side. So it was very important to have this road and railway under control. This area forms at the same time the link to the coast, and it was a major weapons supply line. I mentioned earlier on that there was an arms embargo on the countries of the former Yugoslavia and -- but, of course, the arms embargo was broken. Many parts and weapons usually came from Croatian and then they were transported on this line. So this was another reason to get weapons from Croatian through this line, why this road was very important, especially when it came to the first military attempts to lift the siege of Sarajevo and get access to the Bosnian capital. Konjic itself was also an important military centre. About 55 per cent of the Bosnian military industry, defence industry, was located in the Republic of Bosnia, and most of this in its central part. The largest military industrial enterprise was the so-called united specific purpose industry in Sarajevo. This huge defence industry had about 60 large and small plants located throughout the former Yugoslavia, and one of them was the Igman factory of arms and ammunition in Konjic town. There were other military industrial centres in other parts of Bosnia but Igman was one of the largest armaments plants in Bosnia, and it produced ammunition up to 20 mm. It produced mines and other things. It was built underground, and it covers about 20,000 square metres. Control over this factory was, of course, a pre-condition to control over the local defence production, and it was of paramount importance for the Bosnian Army that was under-equipped. I took this information from an article which I have also included in this binder, an article by Milan Vego. He is a specialist in military developments in the former Yugoslavia. This is from the Jane's Intelligence Review. It is published and it is document number 45. There are some more details. I have not time to explain on this here. There were also other objects of military interest in this area. This is my document 44, which I am showing here. So I mentioned Konjic as a town where important defence industry was located. Other objects of high interest to the warring factions were the weapons storage. According to TO's strategy of all people's defence, weapons were stored at the local level in the country and they were supposed to be used by the territorial defence organisation of the republics in the case of a war. So the weapons of the territorial defence of Konjic and of the municipalities of Prozor and Jablanica were stored in the Ljuta Barracks. The Ljuta Barracks are here. It had a similar underground structure as the Igman factory, and this can also be seen in the document by Milan Vego. We find other military facilities in this area like the JNA barracks of Celebici. Konjic municipality is located in the mountainous part of Herzegovina and it is sparsely populated and let us say maybe even economically a weak area with the exception of Konjic town. There are reserves, even rich reserves, of iron ore and several other important goods located in this area. I just would like to mention that Yugoslavia -- in Yugoslavia was a very, very serious economic crisis, that aggravated throughout 1991 and 1992. Bosnia's national product was down 45 per cent from its 1990 level in 1991, so it had reduced by nearly one half. The inflation rate in 1991 was above 1000 per cent, and 30 per cent of people were registered as being unemployed. So the economic crisis was, in fact, deepening. There were many people that did not earn enough money to -- enough money for subsistence. There was a rapid drop in the standards of living in the income. There was growing unemployment and so on. In Konjic there were about 10,000 people employed, most in factories, but these factories had not enough contracts any more, so the economic crisis was also very present in this municipality. About half of the employed in Konjic municipality were employed in factories, and these factories, as I was indicating, did not function any more as they were supposed to do. I believe that the fact that more and more Bosnians found themselves living below the poverty level contributed very negatively to the tension and also to the hostilities that had emerged at this time in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now what happened on the political side in this municipality? Diagram document number 46 shows us composition of the Municipal Assembly in 1990 after the elections. It is in a way similar to the results of elections on the republican level. People tended to vote according to their ethnic affiliation. So we can see that out of 60 seats in the Assembly, the Muslim SDA -- can we see this? -- 60 seats: 28 for the SDA; 14 for the HDZ; and 9 for the Serbs. There were, of course, nine other seats for the three parties altogether: the former Communist, the Alliance of the Reformed Forces, and one to the Union of Socialist Youth. All over Bosnia and also in Konjic municipalities the administrative structures started to disintegrate in 1991. This was a process that happened also in the administrative bodies of this municipality. It happened also within the territorial defence organisation. The territorial defence organisation, together with other forces, became, as I was pointing out, the Bosnian Army, but many local TO commanders of Serb origin did not join this territorial defence and later the Bosnian Army, but they refused to do so, and many Bosnian Croats also refused to do so and the Bosnian Croats joined then the HVO. From March 1992 throughout BH local authorities formed so-called crisis staffs or war staffs. They were already expecting that conflicts might erupt. So I would say after the referendum marked such a critical moment in the history, political history, of this country. These bodies -- let me say what local authorities were at that time. Local authorities meant members of the local administration for higher level. It meant representatives of the political parties, but it meant also chiefs of factories, of the water supply system, of the police and it meant sometimes also military representatives. These crisis staffs, bodies, if you want, were established to control all levels of municipal life, including the police, finance, communications and so on, and they were preparing to take control as soon as hostilities erupted. We can see this in many municipalities throughout Bosnia. There were marked differences as to how these crisis staffs were functioning, as to how they were composed, but this was, in fact, the case in many municipalities, that these kind of underground structures were emerging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I understand it in the way that all the three groups, the three parties had their own crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had more or less their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the one who then took control had a crisis staff ready and the others on the losing side could not use their crisis staff any more, at least in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It depended, of course, which group was in majority. It was easier in regions where one or two groups had a clear majority, and they were -- as maybe in Konjic already, they hold already the majority of positions and of seats in the Assembly. Then it was clear that they were the most important members to participate then in these crisis staffs, and of course there were other examples, especially in communities which were taken by military action, how these staffs came into being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the member of a crisis staff in Konjic, for instance, could also be sitting working on the existing municipality levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. I now elaborate a bit more on this. Especially on the civilian side of these war preparations which started in March and then were intensified, of course, in April when the state of imminent war danger was declared, proclaimed by the Bosnian Presidency. By March 1992 administrative bodies of Konjic had ceased to function. The Serb representatives had withdrawn from the Executive Council, and also from the Municipal Assembly. In April 1992 this mentioned crisis staff was formalised into a local government. It was called "War Presidency". This institution of a War Presidency, which was then at the time the most important civilian authority at the time, was an institution which was already invented in the system of all people's defence, so it was in a way a heritage coming from the old Yugoslav times. Let me show the law on all people's defence of Bosnia of 1983, my document number 47, and I will put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. After Bosnia-Herzegovina declared independence, did it immediately have a constitution of its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry? No, it did not have a constitution. It had the old Bosnian constitution of 1974 but the constitution was constantly amended through this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought the most relevant would be the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself but did it have the constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Bosnian government was constantly adding new Articles to this constitution and there was a period of time in 1992 where, in fact, there was a kind of chaotic situation from the legal point of view and also from the point of view how these laws and how the Articles of the constitution were, in fact, implemented, because it was just so much confusion about which law was still there and which law should not be applicable any more. This also creates now a lot of confusion for persons who have to analyse what was really going on from the legal point of view during this time. So we have to consider, I think, as well the old Yugoslav legislation and the old constitution but we have also to consider what was then new from the legal point of view are and I will show you both. Let me start now with how the old legislation perceived the War Presidency in times of -- immediate threat of war in times of war. I refer here to the law on all people's defence for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia in 1983, document number 47. We see here in Article 66: "The Presidency of the Municipal Assembly", which is the War Presidency, "shall be established in time of war or in the event of an immediate threat of war." This War Presidency, as we can see from the same Article: "... shall lead all people's resistance in the territory of the municipality. It shall make decisions about issues which fall within the sphere of competence of the Municipal Assembly, should the Assembly not be able to convene." This was in many municipalities of Bosnia the case, especially in the ethnically mixed area. So it could not meet any more. War Presidencies were established and also in Konjic this kind of War Presidency was established. So who was now supposed to be a member of this? Article 67, which is -- 67 starts on this page -- tells us that the Presidency is composed of the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly and a certain number of members. A certain number of members says the Article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It sounds a bit unprecise to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It sounds a bit unprecise. I will explain later on a bit more that it was, in fact, not too unprecise. It was flexible but not unprecise. Let us see here. There are more members named in the same Article. For instance, the President of the Municipal Assembly; the President of the Council; the President of the Committee of the League of Communists. At this time that was the only party, the main party. Then we have representatives of labour unions. We have war veterans and again we have other members of the Presidency, and interestingly under this Article we have also the Commander of the local territorial defence. So under this old Yugoslavian law the War Presidency, which was, in fact, meant to be a civilian body, was composed of all relevant persons in a certain local environment, starting from administration, including also people coming from the factories or water supply or whatever, and also representatives from the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence in this matter is: "Other members of the Presidency shall appointed by ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. So there was a possibility to appoint members according to local conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was this Municipal Assembly functioning at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not -- you mean in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Konjic in the Spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Assembly was not functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not functioning. So this was the old law. The Bosnian government in May 1992 passed a new Defence Law, and this Defence Law had also an Article on War Presidencies and it was a bit different from the old Yugoslavia, the old Bosnian socialist law. This was, of course, normal, because the conditions had changed completely, and the needs and also the composition of this War Presidency had to be changed. I, therefore, present the new Defence Law of May, especially the Article 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now under number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are number 48, Article 40, telling us the composition according to the new law. It was again the Chairman of the Municipal Assembly, the Executive Council, representative of the Ministry of Defence, the Chief of Police and the Commander of the Civil Defence, and also the Chairman of the political party factions. To make it a bit more clear, I produced a diagram, which is document number 49. So this is the composition of the War Presidency according to the Defence Law of Bosnia in May 1992. Just a little bit more to be reduced, please, otherwise you cannot see it. Okay. So, interesting under this new law, the representative of the territorial defence, which means the representative of the armed forces, was not any longer supposed to be a member of this War Presidency. So it formally on paper became a pure civilian body, with the President, so the highest authority of the municipality, representative of the civil defence staff, the President of the government, named Executive Council, the Head of Police, Head of Public Security Service, representative of the Defence Ministry coming from Sarajevo, and the representatives of the political parties in specific municipalities. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just ask you, before we leave this, the law is of 20th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it enter into force immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did enter into force immediately. However, it was not implemented in most of the municipalities, and it was not implemented in Konjic until September 1992. So I cannot really conclude who exactly the members of this civilian, highest civilian body, were, and I assume it was a very flexible system of composition. I cannot confirm that the composition was according to the old law, and I can neither confirm that it was according to this law. What I know is this law was implemented in September 1992. There was a period of like a vacuum and maybe changing persons participating in the work of the War Presidency. What was the War Presidency supposed to do? Organise the local defence logistically according to the doctrine of all people's defence. They were, of course, involved in many, many security-related matters, for instance, arms supply; for instance, recruitment of soldiers; and other war or defence-related tasks. So this was the civilian organisation under the law of the Bosnian constitution and under the law of the -- Defence Law of 20th May 1992. So what happened now on the military side? I just wanted to mention one thing. I was saying under the new law the Territorial Defence was not supposed to be represented in this War Presidency. However, we have here the Head of the Security Service, the Head of police, and under the same Defence Law the police in times of war was supposed to become a part of the armed forces. So this person, Head of Security, Head of Police, was in a way the link, the institutional link between the civilian and the military side, and again I cannot -- I do not know who exactly the members at this time were. So on the military side let us remember that the Bosnian government was trying to build up the new army, the Bosnian Army, and they were trying to streamline the organisation all over the territory of Bosnia, and of course in some areas this was easier and in some areas it was completely impossible. The armed forces consisted -- included also the police and other security forces. This is what I was just explaining before. So what was the situation in April and May 1992? The situation was difficult, of course, for the Bosnian government. Sarajevo was besieged by Serb troops. The communications were interrupted with much of the rest of the territory and the local armed forces, the former TO, which was to become the Bosnian Army often operated under the command of local officers. I show you another diagram, the diagram 51, the organisational structure of the army of the Republic of Bosnia in Spring 1992. This is how it should have looked like, but it does not work, of course in that way. According to the already mentioned law on all people's defence, and according also to the new Defence Law there were three levels within the organisation of the Bosnian army. There was, of course, the republican level, so the headquarters in Sarajevo; there was then a district level; and there was a municipal level. So we have three levels. So at this time the HQ in Sarajevo, of course, was effectively working. However, they did not manage to establish headquarters in all the cities where they wanted. The headquarters in Mostar would not be established at that early time for different reasons. There were internal problems going on in this municipality. Croats and Muslims are not in agreement. The armed forces were not in agreement on establishing such a headquarters. So in a way we should just bear in mind that this did not function as it should. It was in the mind of the commanders but not in reality. The HQ in Konjic, which was established at this time, was more or less acting independently, and there remains a question mark as to whether they had a direct line, of course, to the headquarters in Sarajevo, which may have been the case, but I also can imagine there were many decisions taken autonomously in this area. So what I was trying to say is in this early period, the first months after the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia, the normal chain of command, supreme command -- supreme command, district headquarters, municipal headquarters, and then the units which came under them was interrupted and they were interrupted here on the district level, and I guess they were often interrupted even here on this level, as I was saying. The capital was besieged and it was not easy often to get communications through from here to the different levels. From April 1992 onwards the Konjic Territorial Defence Organisation, which was later to become the Bosnian Army, formed a joint command with the HVO. The Croats had established their own headquarters in the municipality of Konjic. Croats and the TO forces formed at that time a joint staff. The TO Commander was the Commander of the joint staff and the HVO Commander was the Deputy Commander of the staff. This structure, however, did not result always in an integrated command structure. In reality it often happened that decisions were taken jointly by the commanders of each military formation, and also the police forces participated somehow in this military structure. Let me come to a very important document from the Yugoslav army from before the war. It is a document on the strategy of all people's defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 52?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under number 52. It explains how leadership should function in times of war. It shows us in reality how flexible this system was. "Leadership is organised so that the transition to operations during emergencies and in a war requires minor structural and organisational changes. All leadership structures must make their decisions within their jurisdiction and in their field and area according to general aims and specific circumstances, with the purpose of finding appropriate solutions, even when no orders have been received from higher authorities." This document on all people's defence is a secret document where the statutory of all people's defence was established in 1987, and it explains to us de facto local commanders should have a relatively high level of competence and of independence and in this situation they just could not get the orders from their superiors. So it continues in the same sense: "Leadership of all people's defence in peacetime, emergencies and in wartime is arranged organisationally and functionally so that it enables the leadership to take the initiative in organising and performing various forms and means of defence activity. Acting according to the directions of higher authorities ... is the basic principle of the functioning and the leadership system ... But", and now I think it is gets very important, "since the activities of all people's defence are distributed throughout society, the leadership of those activities establishes not only relations of subordination, but also those of cooperation and coordination. Within that framework all sub-systems, elements and parts of systems which are positioned lower in the hierarchy of leadership have to seek opportunities to demonstrate their own initiative and their own contribution to the efficiency of the system as a whole." So really this document really places a high degree of responsibility to the local commanders, and it was perceived in a way that many of the local commanders and persons should contribute to make this system function, all people's defence, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It looks to me as if it is a very open mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is like a very open mandate, especially then as summarised in the last paragraph of this document: "Leadership is decentralised to the extent which allows the required degree of unity. The decentralised system of leadership creates a division of responsibility." So a division of responsibility: "But neither the responsibility of the parts for their own activity nor their responsibility for the activity of the whole system is thus diminished or questioned." So very interesting document from old Yugoslavia. It was this strategy of all people's defence and self protection of the SFRY and I think it explains then what happened throughout Bosnia. It was very flexible, it was very open, and this also included in many instances that personal relationships, informal contacts based on friendship, kinship and so on -- and similar were often maybe more important than holding an official appointment, having rank or following a formal chain of command. It was also, in fact -- it was also the fact that in many parts of Bosnia and also in many other parts of Yugoslavia new personalities, new elites emerged in this situation of total social, political and also economic change. Persons with influence, with credibility, skills and of course economic power could assume responsibility in the civilian structure, but also often in the military hierarchy persons were often appointed positions on an ad hoc basis according to local needs and conditions. For example it was also common and regulated by a decree with force of law for civilians to be appointed to specific positions within the military structure. This statement is supported by document number 53: "Decree on Service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 1992". There we can have this regulated, that also. If need be, non-military persons could perform functions in this system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The thing you now stated on people with influence or money or strong personality or whatever it might be -- have you made these observations not only at Konjic but also in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In many municipalities in many parts not only of Bosnia but also Croatia and Serbia. I mean, there were persons like leaders of paramilitary formations. Arkan is a prominent example. It might also refer to even prominent persons like Fikret Abdic, who was a member even of the State Presidency, but he was also economically in a very strong position in the area of Bihac. He was often described as a person who had much influence and power, at least in this area, due to economic achievements, to good relations, to his personal capabilities. So there are really many examples, and also on all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you now say pertains to all the three parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It pertains to all the three parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbians, Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It pertains to all the three parties. This also means in reality the composition and also the competence of many institutions. The civilian but also the military institutions were highly unclear, and they are especially -- from looking from outside they were often unclear, and there were big differences from one municipality to the next. It is, to summarise, not always entirely clear from the existing legislation which functions were being performed by different organs or by individuals at the local level, especially during the early period of 1991/1992, and we have always to bear in mind that the conditions for which the defence system had been invented were now no longer in place, that they were changing dramatically, especially during the first months. All institutions had split along ethnic lines and the idea to have a unified defence system was completely out of reality during that time. So what happened in the early months of 1992? I am, of course, not a fact witness, so I cannot testify on the military events happening, but apparently there were during April and May 1992 armed conflicts between the Territorial Defence Organisation, later the Bosnian Army, on the one hand, conducted together with the Croat HVO, together with paramilitary forces coming from Croatia, coming also from the Muslim side, and JNA forces on the other side. The JNA had, prior to those conflicts, mobilised volunteers in this area. They had also distributed weapons among them. I have got a document number 54 elaborating on this, explaining this. This is a document by the JNA of Bosnia to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia in Belgrade in March 1992. This is the evidence for what I was saying. JNA mobilised Serbs, distributed weapons. However, we have to have in mind that the JNA had no specific interest in this area of Konjic. They had specific interest in many other parts of Bosnia in the North and in the eastern part, but not so much in this Central part, and we can also read this from the very same documents. We can understand from these documents that in Konjic JNA was preparing to withdraw and they were even trying to take on the arms they had stored there to parts of Bosnia where the Serbs were in majority, and which were under Serb control, but they apparently did not manage. I could conclude that during April 1992 and May 1992 the Croat and the Muslim forces managed to take over most of the significant points and installations in the municipality, parts of them by military action, and we know about this by two reports by the United Nations' commissions of experts established pursuant to Security Council Resolution 780, a very basic document on what was going on in the former Yugoslavia. So the two annexes, annex 3A and annex 8, here included as document number 33 and document number 55, explain some of the military events going on in the early -- in this early time, so that we have at least an independent body testifying on these events. If I had to characterise the first months, April, May 1992 and maybe part of June, the first months -- if I had to characterise them, I would say there was a power vacuum on the republican level, a power vacuum that allowed the local authorities in the municipality, the civilian authorities as well as the military authorities, to act nearly independently from the rest. There was also a certain continuity of power structures from before the war. For instance, this institution of War Presidency was introduced earlier on, but it still existed as an institution. However, this whole system was highly flexible. It adapted to the changing circumstances, and it allowed to integrate new elements and persons wherever needed, and this fitted completely perfectly in the idea in the doctrine of the Yugoslav all people's defence. From the summer onwards, from the early summer onwards, the focus of military interest of the Bosnian Army shifted away from the Konjic municipality. The Bosnian Presidency planned to lift the Serb siege of Sarajevo, which required major support from other areas, and it required also support from Konjic. Konjic, as I was saying, at this time was nearly completely under control of the Muslim and of the Croat authorities in a civilian and military sense. So there was certain room for manoeuvre to supply or to contribute to the effort, to the military effort in other areas. The army of Bosnia at this time established a tactical group to lift the siege of Sarajevo. I am again not a fact witness on tactical groups or who was a member or a commander, or how it was composed. I can just explain in general what a tactical group was. I have got two documents and I will use here only one. They are saying basically the same things. I use document number 36. This is the Military Lexicon published in Belgrade in 1991. It has a short paragraph on tactical groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical groups, in our file number 36.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Tactical group: Temporary combined unit intended for combat activities in a separate tactical direction when a certain combat task cannot be carried out in the zone or direction of the activities with a formation unit". So it is first formed just to fulfil a very specific, a clearly defined task. It can be a military task; it can also be support, supply. It can be maybe a tactical group. So they had a specific purpose, specific task: "It is formed within combined tactical units and it acts independently as a part of the combat structure of the unit. It is assigned separate command or it is commanded by the command that set it up. The strength and composition of the tactical group depends on the strength and the composition of the unit that is setting it up, the task, as well as on the characteristics of the terrain, the site of the zone and strength and composition of the enemy". So this tactical group at this time, Tactical Group Number 1, was established to take military action to lift the siege of Sarajevo. It was not successful at this time, but again I am not a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you studied in any way how tactical groups function in other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am not an expert in military things. I know that there were other tactical groups. I know especially about one in eastern Bosnia in this early period, eastern parts of Bosnia, but I cannot testify or I cannot give any expertise on how they were composed, which tasks they were exactly performing, what their aim was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How they functioned in general, etc. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
